title: Symmetry
wiki_lead:
In everyday life, symmetry (from Ancient Greek  συμμετρία (summetría) 'agreement in dimensions, due proportion, arrangement') refers to a sense of harmonious and beautiful proportion and balance. In mathematics, the term has a more precise definition and is usually used to refer to an object that is invariant under some transformations, such as translation, reflection, rotation, or scaling. Although these two meanings of the word can sometimes be told apart, they are intricately related, and hence are discussed together in this article.
Mathematical symmetry may be observed with respect to the passage of time; as a spatial relationship; through geometric transformations; through other kinds of functional transformations; and as an aspect of abstract objects, including theoretic models, language, and music.
This article describes symmetry from three perspectives: in mathematics, including geometry, the most familiar type of symmetry for many people; in science and nature; and in the arts, covering architecture, art, and music.
The opposite of symmetry is asymmetry, which refers to the absence of symmetry.

This article describes symmetry from three perspectives: in mathematics, including geometry, the most familiar type of symmetry for many people; in science and nature; and in the arts, covering architecture, art, and music.
The opposite of symmetry is asymmetry, which refers to the absence of symmetry.


In mathematics


In geometry

A geometric shape or object is symmetric if it can be divided into two or more identical pieces that are arranged in an organized fashion. This means that an object is symmetric if there is a transformation that moves individual pieces of the object, but doesn't change the overall shape. The type of symmetry is determined by the way the pieces are organized, or by the type of transformation:

An object has reflectional symmetry (line or mirror symmetry) if there is a line (or in 3D a plane) going through it which divides it into two pieces that are mirror images of each other.
An object has rotational symmetry if the object can be rotated about a fixed point (or in 3D about a line) without changing the overall shape.
An object has translational symmetry if it can be translated (moving every point of the object by the same distance) without changing its overall shape.
An object has helical symmetry if it can be simultaneously translated and rotated in three-dimensional space along a line known as a screw axis.
An object has scale symmetry if it does not change shape when it is expanded or contracted. Fractals also exhibit a form of scale symmetry, where smaller portions of the fractal are similar in shape to larger portions.
Other symmetries include glide reflection symmetry (a reflection followed by a translation) and rotoreflection symmetry (a combination of a rotation and a reflection).


In logic
A dyadic relation R = S × S is symmetric if for all elements a, b in S, whenever it is true that Rab, it is also true that Rba. Thus, the relation "is the same age as" is symmetric, for if Paul is the same age as Mary, then Mary is the same age as Paul.
In propositional logic, symmetric binary logical connectives include and (∧, or &), or (∨, or |) and if and only if (↔), while the connective if (→) is not symmetric. Other symmetric logical connectives include nand (not-and, or ⊼), xor (not-biconditional, or ⊻), and nor (not-or, or ⊽).


Other areas of mathematics

Generalizing from geometrical symmetry in the previous section, one can say that a mathematical object is symmetric with respect to a given mathematical operation, if, when applied to the object, this operation preserves some property of the object. The set of operations that preserve a given property of the object form a group.
In general, every kind of structure in mathematics will have its own kind of symmetry. Examples include even and odd functions in calculus, symmetric groups in abstract algebra, symmetric matrices in linear algebra, and Galois groups in Galois theory. In statistics, symmetry also manifests as symmetric probability distributions, and as skewness—the asymmetry of distributions.

grok_lead: Symmetry is a fundamental concept across mathematics, physics, and other disciplines, denoting the invariance of an object, system, or law under specific transformations such as rotations, reflections, translations, or scalings, where the essential properties remain unchanged. This property allows for balanced and proportionate structures that appear identical before and after the transformation, as exemplified by a circle that looks the same after any rotation. In mathematics, symmetry is rigorously analyzed through group theory, which classifies symmetries as elements of a group under composition of transformations; common types include reflection symmetry (mirror-like invariance across a line or plane), rotational symmetry (invariance under turns around a point or axis), translational symmetry (invariance under shifts in position), and glide reflection (a combination of reflection and translation). These symmetries form the basis for studying geometric figures, patterns, and even abstract algebraic structures, enabling the prediction of object behavior under transformations. Historically, the mathematical exploration of symmetry traces back to ancient Greek geometry, but its modern formalization emerged in the 19th century with the development of group theory by mathematicians like Ãvariste Galois. In physics, symmetry principles govern the fundamental laws of nature, dictating that physical systems and their governing equations remain unaltered under certain changes, such as shifts in time or space. A cornerstone is Noether's theorem, proved in 1918 by Emmy Noether, which establishes that every differentiable symmetry of the action of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity, linking rotational symmetry to conservation of angular momentum, translational symmetry to conservation of linear momentum, and time symmetry to conservation of energy. These symmetries are essential in quantum mechanics, relativity, and particle physics, where they predict phenomena like the stability of atoms and the uniformity of fundamental forces. However, symmetry breaking âwhere a symmetric system spontaneously adopts an asymmetric stateâexplains diverse natural occurrences, such as the alignment of magnetic domains or the Higgs mechanism that gives particles mass. Beyond science, symmetry manifests prominently in nature and human endeavors, often evoking aesthetic appeal and functional efficiency. In biology, bilateral symmetry predominates in animals for streamlined movement and sensory organization, while radial symmetry appears in organisms like starfish and jellyfish to optimize environmental interaction. Empirical studies show a cross-cultural human preference for symmetric patterns in faces and shapes, often attributed to evolutionary advantages such as signaling health in mate selection. In art and architecture, artists harness symmetry to achieve visual harmony and proportion, as seen in classical Greek temples or Islamic geometric designs, where it symbolizes order and beauty across cultures. Overall, symmetry not only unifies disparate fields but also underscores the elegance and predictability inherent in the universe.
